grades.quote: Recall that the inode functions require the caller to handle locking
grades.reason: Covers the file-descriptor layer. Its reference count is on struct file, not on inodes. It only notes that inode functions leave locking to the caller and that inode locking makes offset updates atomic. This gives limited auxiliary context and does not explain why inode refcounts and locks are separate.

grades.quote: iput() doesn’t truncate a file immediately when the link count for the file drops to zero, because some process might still hold a reference to the inode in memory
grades.reason: Shows that an in-memory reference keeps an inode alive after its link count reaches zero, so references govern lifetime. It says nothing about inode locks or why the two mechanisms are separate, so it is only partly relevant.

Describes the file system interface, including links, unlink, and inodes. It does not discuss inode in-memory reference counts or inode locks. The link-count and file-descriptor remark is background at most.

grades.quote: The function of the lock is to force other uses to wait, not to pin a piece of data to a particular agent.
grades.reason: Gives the general xv6 principle behind the separation. A lock forces other users to wait and does not pin data to an agent (it can be held across sleeps, as with ilock's acquiresleep). Reference counts decide when an object can be freed, since holding a lock does not guarantee that freeing is safe. It does not discuss inode reference counts directly (pipes are the example), so the answer is only partial.
